head: Brazil's Pantanal national park is about a third larger than it was.
summary: Brazil has added roughly 48,000 hectares — about 185 square miles — of wetland and riverside forest to Pantanal Matogrossense National Park, taking it from some 135,000 hectares to 183,095. The Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation, which runs the park, chose the new ground along the corridors animals already use to move in and out, and is working with neighbouring landowners on buffer zones either side of them. The park sits in the world's largest flooded grassland, counted home to 463 bird species, 269 kinds of fish and the densest population of jaguars anywhere, along with giant otters, giant armadillos and marsh deer.

head: A dry forest above Ethiopia's Rift Valley has been named a UN restoration flagship.
summary: The UN Environment Programme gave the Desa'a landscape World Restoration Flagship status on October 29 at the biodiversity conference in Yerevan, recognising more than 23,000 hectares of degraded ground now being brought back on the escarpment above the Great Rift Valley. Work started in 2016 with the forest charity WeForest and is now run by the communities living there; measurements credit it with holding back about 500,000 tonnes of soil, catching some 1.9 million cubic metres of rainwater a year, and lifting water infiltration in treated ground by 26 percent since 2019 while untreated ground fell 40 percent. Beekeeping and wider tree cover come next, and UNEP reckons the landscape could take up around 6 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent over 50 years.

place: Coffs Harbour hinterland, New South Wales, Australia
head: New South Wales has turned 178,000 hectares of state forest into a koala park.
summary: The state parliament passed the bill creating the Great Koala National Park on October 23, folding 178,000 hectares of state forest and other public land into reserves already standing in the hinterland behind Coffs Harbour, for a park of about 475,000 hectares. Most of that forest had been set aside for native timber harvesting; it holds roughly 12,000 koalas and more than a hundred other threatened species, among them southern greater gliders, glossy black cockatoos and rare spider orchids. The government has put A$140 million towards establishing the park, which is due to open before the end of the year, and the National Parks Association of New South Wales — which ran the ten-year campaign for it — is already making the case for two excluded state forests to be added.

head: Barbados has gone three years without a baby born with HIV.
summary: The World Health Organization certified Barbados on October 30 for eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HIV, after an independent review found that no infant born in the country between 2022 and 2024 had acquired the virus from their mother. Across those three years, 98 percent of pregnant women received antenatal care, 98 percent were tested for HIV, and 98 percent of those living with it were on antiretroviral treatment. Barbados is one of 26 countries and territories WHO now recognises for this, fifteen of them in the Americas, and the third this year after the Bahamas and Turks and Caicos.

head: Senegal starts manufacturing the world's first rapid test for measles.
summary: Gavi approved deployment of the first-ever rapid diagnostic test for measles on September 30, 2026, with production based in Dakar, Senegal. DIATROPIX, a manufacturing subsidiary of the Institut Pasteur de Dakar, makes the test, which cleared a rigorous evaluation by WHO and was validated by the Public Health Agency of Canada's National Microbiology Laboratory. Up to 500,000 tests a year are expected to roll out starting in Senegal, giving frontline health workers a faster way to confirm outbreaks and direct vaccination campaigns where they're needed most.

head: Five countries and territories in the Americas were recognised for eliminating diseases, Chile's rabies among them.
summary: The Pan American Health Organization honoured Brazil, Chile, El Salvador, the Bahamas and Turks and Caicos on September 29 for eliminating mother-to-child HIV transmission, leprosy, trachoma and more. Chile became the first country in South America validated for eliminating dog-transmitted rabies this month, and about 60 percent of places worldwide recognised for ending mother-to-child HIV transmission are in the Americas. The region aims to eliminate more than 30 communicable diseases by 2030.

head: The High Seas Treaty passed 100 member countries in a single week.
summary: Germany, Papua New Guinea, Zimbabwe, Canada, Australia and Brunei Darussalam deposited their ratifications during UN General Assembly week, taking the treaty past 100 parties on September 23. It gives the waters beyond national borders, nearly half the planet's surface, their first shared legal framework for conservation, and has been in force since 17 January 2026. Parties meet for the first time in January 2027, when they will begin deciding where the first high-seas protected areas go.

head: The WHO widened its safety checklist for medical devices worldwide.
summary: The World Health Organization added condoms, IUDs, and AI-assisted tuberculosis-screening software to its prequalification programme, which vets devices for safety before global procurement. The expansion targets the roughly 70 percent of countries with weak regulatory systems for health products, giving buyers and donors a trusted list to work from. WHO will also take over vetting contraceptive devices from the UN Population Fund, with assessments of the newly added products beginning on a published timeline.

head: Côte d'Ivoire is building a nationwide drone network to keep rural clinics stocked with blood and vaccines.
summary: The Ivorian government approved an eight-year plan to expand Zipline's drone delivery service from one hub in Daloa to ten across the country, eventually reaching more than 2,200 health facilities and 12 million people. The pilot site has already flown 3.55 million medical products, including 20,500 units of blood, to clinics that used to wait days for supply runs over poor roads. Government spokesman Amadou Coulibaly says the expansion is meant to give hard-to-reach communities a "regular and secure supply" of medicine.

head: Benin doubled access to drinking water in five years by taxing itself first.
summary: Access to drinking water across Benin rose from 40 percent to 80 percent of the population over the past five years, the United Nations reported, funded partly through Africa's first sovereign SDG bond, issued in 2021. The West African country raised its domestic tax revenue by 0.5 percent of GDP every year for a decade, then funneled the proceeds into water systems and a new industrial zone that has created 25,000 jobs. Economic cooperation minister Aristide Medenou said the lesson for other countries chasing the 2030 development goals is simple: raise the money at home first.

head: Renewable sources supplied nearly three-quarters of Portugal's electricity this year.
summary: From January through August, 74.4 percent of mainland Portugal's electricity came from renewables, led by near-even shares of solar and wind, according to industry group APREN. The shift avoided an estimated €809 million in natural gas imports and €492 million in carbon-permit costs over the same eight months. Portugal now ranks fourth among the eight European countries APREN tracks, trailing only Norway, Denmark, and Austria.

head: Renewables supplied more than four-fifths of eastern Australia's power for the first time.
summary: At 12:30pm on a Saturday in September, renewables briefly supplied 80.5 percent of the electricity used across Australia's National Electricity Market, which spans the eastern states, breaking a record set just one day earlier. Rooftop solar did much of the work, contributing more than half of the clean-energy mix and peaking at 16,993 megawatts the next day at noon, according to data from analyst Geoff Eldridge. Batteries absorbed 4.46 gigawatts of the surplus and pumped hydro another 880 megawatts, evidence the grid is starting to catch power it once had to curtail.

head: Athens is turning its old airport into one of Europe's largest parks.
summary: The city is converting 400 acres of the former Ellinikon airport on its southern waterfront into a park second in size only to London's Richmond Park. Planners are putting in 30,000 trees and 3 million smaller plants, more than 500 species chosen to keep the grounds roughly 7 degrees Fahrenheit cooler than the surrounding asphalt. The park opens to the public in 2027, with further planting continuing through 2030 under Mayor Haris Doukas.

head: South Africa has gone 490 days without a rolling blackout.
summary: Eskom reported this week that South Africa has run 490 consecutive days without loadshedding since May 2025, while its power plants hit 67.96 percent availability, the highest in six years. Lower unplanned outages and less reliance on diesel generators cut emergency fuel spending by 4.8 billion rand, and 1.4 million customers have had normal supply restored. About 247,617 customers, 3.4 percent of Eskom's base, remain on temporary load reduction as repairs continue.

head: Nine African countries have more than doubled average incomes since 1990.
summary: A new analysis from Our World in Data finds Ghana, Mauritius, Egypt, Cabo Verde, Rwanda, Ethiopia, Uganda, Burkina Faso and Mozambique have all more than doubled average incomes since 1990, with Ghana's rising from about $1,850 to roughly $7,360 per person. Extreme poverty and child mortality fell in all nine countries over the same period. Mauritius leads the group at nearly $28,770 per person, though researchers note the figures are national averages and don't show how the gains are shared within each country.
